name: Gluten-free diet for bloat

lead: A gluten-free diet excludes the proteins in wheat, barley and rye. Among appearance-focused users it is tried to reduce bloating and facial puffiness and to look slimmer through the midsection and face.

For people with celiac disease, gluten triggers an immune reaction in the small intestine, and the diet is the accepted treatment. In non-celiac gluten sensitivity, bloating is a symptom, and a 2018 crossover study suggested fructans may contribute more than gluten. No study of facial appearance was found.

paras: Users swap bread, pasta and baked goods for gluten-free versions or naturally gluten-free foods such as rice, potatoes, meat, vegetables and fruit, and judge the change over a few weeks. Physicians generally advise testing for celiac disease before starting, since the diet can affect test accuracy.

Nutritional gaps are possible, including iron, B vitamins, folate, calcium and fiber, especially when processed gluten-free substitutes replace whole foods. Going gluten-free before testing can mask celiac disease.

angle.text: Users drop gluten hoping for less gut bloating and a slimmer midsection and face. The diet is the accepted treatment for celiac disease, and no studies were found on facial puffiness in people without gluten-related conditions.

lead: A gluten-free diet leaves out gluten, the storage proteins of wheat, barley, rye and related grains. For celiac disease it is the standard treatment, and it is also used for wheat allergy and gluten ataxia. [1] Many people without those diagnoses try it to settle abdominal bloating, since a lower belly that swells after bread or pasta changes how a midsection looks in clothes and in photos. [1][2]

In appearance-focused communities the chain proponents describe is: remove wheat-based foods, have less gut distension and less fluid-feeling puffiness, and show a flatter stomach and a sharper-looking waist and face. Non-celiac gluten sensitivity (NCGS), a label for symptoms that ease off gluten when celiac disease and wheat allergy have been excluded, lists bloating among its digestive symptoms; its prevalence is estimated at 0.5 to 13 percent and whether it is a distinct condition is still debated. [2][3]

Researchers have asked whether the fermentable carbohydrates in wheat, especially fructans, rather than gluten itself, explain bloating, and a low-FODMAP approach is often discussed by clinicians for functional bloating. [1][4][5] The diet became a mainstream lifestyle choice in the early 21st century, helped by popular books such as William Davis's Wheat Belly (2011) and by celebrity and athlete adoption. [1][3][6] Studies of the diet for facial puffiness or appearance in people without a gluten-related diagnosis have not been published.

paras: The diet removes wheat, barley, rye and products made from them, and relies on naturally gluten-free foods or gluten-free substitutes. Pseudocereals such as quinoa, amaranth and buckwheat are described as more nutritious alternatives [1]. Since the early 2000s it has also become a popular lifestyle choice promoted by celebrities and some athletes, and a cited survey found nearly half of 910 athletes followed it, mainly for perceived health and energy benefits [1].

Wikipedia describes the diet as having become a fad diet since the start of the 21st century, promoted by celebrities and some professional athletes for weight loss and energy, while noting it reports no published experimental evidence that a gluten-free diet causes weight loss [1].

Non-celiac gluten sensitivity covers digestive and non-digestive symptoms that appear within hours or days of gluten and fade when it is removed; no biomarker exists to diagnose it, and exclusion of celiac disease and wheat allergy is needed first [2]. A 2018 double-blind study found bloating borderline higher after fructan than after gluten challenges, and experts sometimes suggest a low-FODMAP diet for bloating [1]. A 2022 review of upper gut disorders notes that reported benefits of gluten elimination in functional dyspepsia are confounded by lower intake of wheat fructans and other FODMAPs [4].

The link between wheat and celiac disease was made in the 1940s by Dutch paediatrician Willem Dicke, whose observations during the Dutch famine of 1944 to 1945, when flour was scarce, supported the connection; the gluten fraction was identified in 1952 by a team in Birmingham, England. [7] For decades the diet was a medical treatment for a minority.

Patients without celiac disease whose abdominal pain and diarrhoea improved on a gluten-free diet were described in the late 1970s, with the first case series in 1980. [3] Consensus conferences in London (2011), Munich (2012) and Oslo (2013) later set out diagnostic criteria for NCGS, although many experts still debate whether it is a distinct condition. [3] From the early 2000s the diet spread beyond patients, promoted by celebrities and some professional athletes; a survey cited on Wikipedia found nearly half of 910 athletes following it, mainly for perceived health and energy benefits. [1]

FODMAPs are short-chain carbohydrates, including fructans, galacto-oligosaccharides, lactose, fructose and polyols, that are poorly absorbed in the small intestine and fermented by gut bacteria, producing gas that can cause bloating. [5] Wheat and rye contain fructans, so wheat-free eating lowers FODMAP intake as a side effect. The FODMAP hypothesis was set out by Gibson and Shepherd in 2005 and management guidance followed in 2010. [5]

Several studies report that a low-FODMAP diet improves digestive symptoms in adults with irritable bowel syndrome. [5] Reviews as of 2019 concluded that fructans may explain bloating after wheat but not the extra-digestive symptoms attributed to NCGS. [3] Authors of FODMAP guidance recommend it for short periods under a specialist, with medical evaluation first, and note that long-term restriction may affect the gut microbiota and that it can mask celiac disease symptoms. [5]

Cutting gluten for a flatter stomach is a staple of physique-prep and wellness advice, where bloating is treated as the difference between a visible and an obscured midsection on photo day. Self-diagnosis is common: Wikipedia notes that many people with suspected NCGS have already begun the diet before evaluation, and that some critics describe a fad component to its popularity. [3] Mayo Clinic Proceedings authors likewise note that most suspected cases have started a gluten-free diet by the time they are assessed. [2]

Wheat Belly and similar books argue that modern wheat varieties drive weight gain and a swollen belly; its author says wheat has changed since the 1950s and 1960s. [6] Critics quoted on Wikipedia, including the American Association of Cereal Chemists, report that most studies found no link between refined-grain intake and cardiovascular disease, diabetes, weight gain or mortality. [6] Some users switch to gluten-free versions of bread and snacks, which can be higher in sugar and fat than the wheat products they replace. [1]

Celiac disease affects about 1 to 2 percent of people and is managed by strict gluten exclusion; up to 79 percent have incomplete small-bowel recovery despite a strict diet, mainly from inadvertent exposure, and up to 30 percent of known patients continue to have or redevelop symptoms [1]. A 2007 trial cited by Wikipedia found 10 mg of gluten a day to be the last known safe limit for celiac patients, while about 50 mg daily changed intestinal architecture [1].

Non-celiac gluten sensitivity (NCGS), described in the Mayo Clinic Proceedings review, has an unknown prevalence, overlapping features with celiac disease and wheat allergy, and thought to involve an innate immune mechanism; dietary triggers other than gluten, such as FODMAPs, have also been implicated [2]. The review advises that a gluten elimination diet followed by a monitored open challenge can sometimes document recurrence, and notes that most suspected cases have already started a gluten-free diet by the time they are evaluated [2].

sections.h: What bloating is and how the diet is used
paras: Abdominal bloating is a sensation of fullness or visible distension that people attribute to foods, gas, fluid or gut sensitivity. In appearance terms, the visible effect is a rounder lower abdomen that varies through the day. People who notice it after bread, pasta or other wheat foods remove them as a trial, and some report a flatter midsection within days to weeks; these accounts are individual reports rather than study findings [1][2].

Clinicians who see this complaint often consider FODMAP intake as well as gluten, because wheat contains fructans, and a 2022 gastroenterology review notes that benefits attributed to gluten elimination in functional dyspepsia are confounded by lower FODMAP intake [4].

A narrative review of gluten intolerance and skin disorders reports improvement on a gluten-free diet in dermatitis herpetiformis and psoriasis-related conditions, with inconsistent results in atopic dermatitis [8]. These findings concern specific diagnoses, not general facial appearance.

Replacing wheat products with gluten-free versions can lower intake of iron, B vitamins, folate, calcium and fibre and raise sugar, saturated fat and carbohydrate, since many such products are less fortified [1]. Cross-contamination is described; one study found 32 percent of restaurant foods labeled gluten-free exceeded 20 ppm [1]. Physicians advise testing for celiac disease before going gluten-free so the test is accurate [1][2].

Wikipedia adds that children often overconsume gluten-free products and that many commercial versions are higher in fat and carbohydrates [1]. A cited Columbia University study found 32 percent of restaurant foods labelled gluten-free exceeded 20 ppm gluten [1].

Wikipedia notes that people should be tested for celiac disease before cutting gluten, because antibodies fall within months of going gluten-free and testing may require several weeks of reintroduction; an estimated 70 percent of people with celiac disease remain undiagnosed. [7]

In the US, the Food Allergen Labeling and Consumer Protection Act of 2004 first addressed gluten-free labelling, and the FDA's final rule issued in August 2013 requires products labelled gluten-free to contain no gluten-containing grain ingredients and under 20 ppm gluten [1]. In the EU, gluten-free means 20 ppm or less and 'very low gluten' means 20 to 100 ppm, with gluten among 14 recognised allergens [1]. A 2008 case of nuggets labelled gluten-free that contained gluten is cited as an example of labelling problems [1].

In wellness and physique communities the diet is frequently bundled with other food exclusions in anti-bloat and clean-eating plans, often alongside cutting dairy, alcohol and ultra-processed food. [1] Popular books supplied much of the language: Wheat Belly by cardiologist William Davis, published in 2011, calls modern wheat a chronic poison and became a New York Times bestseller; reviewers, including a 2013 Journal of Cereal Science review cited on Wikipedia, concluded its statements cannot be substantiated from published studies. [6] Dietitians have cited the Wheat Belly diet as an example of a fad diet and note that restrictive versions can be low in B vitamins, calcium and vitamin D. [6]

A 2013 double-blind challenge by Biesiekierski and colleagues in people with irritable bowel syndrome who believed they were gluten sensitive found no difference between gluten and placebo; Wikipedia notes design problems and that whey protein in the control may have caused a similar nocebo effect in everyone. [1][3] A 2015 double-blind crossover trial reported that small amounts of purified wheat gluten triggered gastrointestinal and extra-intestinal symptoms, though it did not establish whether gluten or other wheat proteins such as amylase-trypsin inhibitors were responsible. [1][3]

A 2018 double-blind crossover study of 59 people who followed a gluten-free diet compared gluten, fructans and placebo; bloating was borderline higher after fructans than after gluten (P=0.049) with very small differences, and the fructans came from chicory root rather than wheat. [1][3] Symptom improvement after starting a gluten-free diet may partly reflect a placebo response. [1] A Mayo Clinic review and a 2022 American Journal of Gastroenterology review cover NCGS and dietary approaches to upper gut disorders. [2][4] A narrative review of gluten intolerance and skin disorders reports improvement in dermatitis herpetiformis, mixed results in atopic dermatitis and other conditions. [8] No studies of gluten-free diets for facial puffiness or facial appearance have been published.

lore.intro: Bloating relief is one of the commonest reasons people give for dropping wheat, and the topic is argued through books, celebrity examples and self-experiments. [3][6]
